source.title: Learning With Noisy Labels Over Imbalanced Subpopulations
source.authors: Ming-Cai Chen; Yu Zhao; Bing He; Zong-Bo Han; Jun-Zhou Huang; Bingzhe Wu; Jian-Hua Yao

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; some figures and table content are garbled or flattened.
record.tranche_reason: Tests learning under random label corruption with a different method and metrics, including training and test accuracy across noise rates; it does not test the original memorization setup directly.
record.gate_note: Reports outcomes for models trained on datasets with randomly flipped labels and compares methods. Results for other cited works are not extracted. The study does not test shuffled pixels, Gaussian inputs, explicit regularization claims, or the learning order of real versus random labels.
record.test_reason: The study uses the memorization-based small-loss rationale to motivate noisy-label learning methods, then evaluates noise identification and clean-test performance. It reports no fitting of the supplied random labels, training-error trajectories, or clean-versus-noisy learning order. Its robustness comparisons therefore do not test the claim versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that LLC-based label confidence estimation and refurbish-DRO improve learning with noisy labels and imbalanced subpopulations, particularly worst-group generalization, while remaining competitive on standard noisy-label benchmarks. They do not conclude that their experiments establish random-label memorization.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LLC-based confidence estimation, label refurbishment and DRO with weak-strong augmentation and co-training; evaluates corrupted labels and subpopulation robustness rather than the original random-label memorization recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported test performance varies with dataset, noise rate and symmetric versus asymmetric noise. The paper reports robustness to choices of KNN neighbor count and DRO threshold, but the plotted sensitivity values are figure-only.

fits_no_version.finding: LLC-based label refurbishment and DRO achieve competitive clean-test accuracy under synthetic label noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Noise-aware label correction and robust training can improve generalization on corrupted-label benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed method improves worst-group accuracy over ERM and improved DivideMix on corrupted Waterbirds and CelebA; worst-group accuracy is not monotonic in corruption rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under subpopulation imbalance, noise-robust methods differ in worst-group generalization, and additional label noise need not monotonically reduce worst-group accuracy.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
record.problems: The reported outcomes are test accuracies rather than training error, and there is no chance-level test comparison for complete random labeling. Noise fractions are discrete and below 100%; no convergence-time results are given. Several relevant plots and portions of tables are garbled in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows extracted. Table 2 results for comparator methods are omitted because the text states they are from prior work [20] or elsewhere, not newly produced here; Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 values are garbled/flattened and do not provide recoverable complete per-condition rows for the versions tested.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training error on completely random labels, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative fitting time for true versus random labels and convergence speed as corruption increases.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

Perfect fitting of corrupted training labels together with steadily increasing test error from no corruption through complete randomization. Reported robustness-method test accuracies do not establish this joint behavior.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and generalization after removing these regularizers.
Temporal ordering of learning shared real-data patterns and memorizing noisy labels. The small-loss rationale is invoked, not tested through learning trajectories.

record.verdict_notes: The nonmonotonic worst-group results concern a different outcome from V4's overall test-error trajectory during perfect training-set fitting. They warrant no challenge verdict for V4. E2 concerns CIFAR Table 2 and is incorrectly linked to Waterbirds row R13.

versions.untested_parts: Tests label corruption up to stated noise rates, but does not report a completely random labeling of the entire training set with training error and test error at chance.
Does not report training time or convergence speed as a function of corrupted-label fraction.
Does not test shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Reports test accuracy at discrete noise rates, but does not report perfect training fit or establish smooth degradation across the full range from no noise to all labels corrupted.
Does not test weight decay, dropout, or whether removing them changes random-label fitting or true-label generalization.
Does not measure the order in which real-label patterns and noisy labels are learned over training.

rows.subject: ERM
rows.operation_detail: Compared on corrupted Waterbirds at 25%, 30%, 35%, and 40% random label flips; reports average and worst-group test accuracy.
rows.note: This is a method comparator under explicit subpopulation imbalance; no training error or clean-label reference is reported in this table.
rows.check: ERM clean-test average/worst-group accuracy measures generalization under noise and imbalance, without establishing training-label memorization. Results use validation-selected checkpoints; split the bundled noise rates and measures if retained.
